newsitem.title: UK: Aerospace insurers face shift to satellites - expert.
newsitem.headline: Aerospace insurers face shift to satellites - expert.

text.p: Aerospace insurers will have to adapt to fewer launch vehicles, but a rise in satellites in orbit around the earth, Simon Clapham, a leading aerospace underwriter said on Thursday.
Launch frequency will start to tail off in five to six years time, as many satellites now operate for 15 years or more, Clapham said in a talk to the Insurance Institute of London.
However, the number of satellites in space will increase, as usage of satellite communication for television, telephone, internet and other applications mushrooms.

Demand for satellite in orbit insurance is expected to match this growth, Clapham said, noting that the value of a satellite rises once it is in space, where it has considerable revenue generating ability.
Another factor set to fuel demand for satellite insurance is the spread of privatisation, which will see satellite operation pass increasingly from state to private hands.
Private owners and their financial backers are more likely to pass risk onto insurers than governments, Clapham said.
However, calculating the risk of damage to satellites in space is still in its infancy, due to the short period for which loss data is available, he added.
International insurers can currently provide up to $900 million cover for each launch vehicle, compared with $350 million maximum capacity for a satellite.
Clapham, who is underwriter for Lloyds of London's Hill syndicate 800 and the Marham Space Consortium, said he represents around $75 million of aerospace insurance.
Other big players are Munich Re, Generali, USAIG and French insurers.
